mainTopic: End of ברכת הלבנה, then the close of פרק היו בודקין: witnesses' timing, the student who argues for acquittal, judges and wine, a deadlocked court, and נזדקן הדין
overview: The amud opens by finishing the discussion of ברכת הלבנה. Both time limits are readings of רבי יוחנן. The moon gets no הטוב והמטיב because its changes are its normal nature. Saying the ברכה on time is like greeting the שכינה, so אביי rules that it is said standing. רב יהודה's full text of the ברכה is given. After a short teaching that winning the 'war' of Torah needs 'bundles' of משנה, the גמרא returns to the משנה. Witnesses who disagree about before sunrise versus during sunrise have void testimony. A student who argues for acquittal stays seated all day when his point is weak. Judges avoid wine because they deal with 'the secret of the world.' A court that stays deadlocked sets the defendant free. The amud ends by explaining the phrase נזדקן הדין, read either as 'the case is stuck' or 'the case has grown wise.' Then the הדרן closes פרק היו בודקין.

steps.title: Both opinions follow רבי יוחנן, but read him differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב יעקב בר אידי (7 days) and the scholars of נהרדעא (16 days) both follow רבי יוחנן. They only disagree about which stage of the moon he meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both of them hold like רבי יוחנן. One says he meant until the moon looks like a bow with its string. The other says he meant until it looks like a round sieve.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is settling an earlier disagreement about how many days into the month one may still say ברכת הלבנה. It shows both sides are really explaining the same rule of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said the ברכה can be said until the moon's 'flaw is filled.' One side understands this as the half-moon, about 7 days in, when it looks like a bow with its string. The other side understands it as the full round moon, about 16 days in.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains where the different time limits for ברכת הלבנה come from. Both are readings of one source, רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: And both of them hold like Rabbi Yochanan:
phrases.notes: Both of them means רב יעקב בר אידי and the scholars of נהרדעא, from just before this.

phrases.english: this one: until it becomes like a bowstring,
phrases.notes: Picture a half-moon: the curved edge is the bow, and the straight edge is its string.

phrases.english: that one: until it becomes like a sieve.
phrases.notes: A sieve is round, so this means the full moon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Wraps up the dispute from the previous section by tying both views to רבי יוחנן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Both opinions share one source but read its wording differently.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the two time limits are unrelated, conflicting opinions.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both explain רבי יוחנן's 'until the flaw is filled.' One reads it as the half-moon and the other as the full moon.

steps.title: Why not say הטוב והמטיב on the moon?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדיפתי suggests that, since people benefit from the moon's light, we should say הטוב והמטיב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא from דיפתי said to רבינא: Let us say the ברכה 'Who is good and does good'!
steps.whatsHappening: A new question opens. רב אחא מדיפתי asks why the moon doesn't get the ברכה of הטוב והמטיב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הטוב והמטיב is said over good news or a benefit. רב אחא reasons that the moon growing back brings light, which is a good thing, so maybe this ברכה should apply.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Who is good and does good,' a ברכה said over good news

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina:
So let one bless 'Who is good and does good'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the timing of ברכת הלבנה to which ברכה fits the moon.
steps.kashyaTarget: The practice of saying only the regular ברכת הלבנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The moon gives a real benefit, and benefits usually call for הטוב והמטיב.

steps.title: We don't say דיין האמת when it shrinks either
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that we don't say דיין האמת when the moon shrinks, so there is no reason to say הטוב והמטיב when it grows.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: When the moon is shrinking, do we say 'the true Judge'? If not, why should we say 'Who is good and does good' when it grows?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא pushes back with a comparison. The bad ברכה isn't said when the moon shrinks, so the good ברכה isn't said when it grows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דיין האמת is said over bad news, and הטוב והמטיב over good news, so they are a matched pair. Since nobody says the bad one for the shrinking moon, the moon's changes are not treated as news, and the good one doesn't fit either.

keyTerms.meaning: is that to say...? (a rhetorical question)
'the true Judge,' a ברכה said over bad news

phrases.english: He said to him:
Is that to say that when it shrinks
do we bless 'the true Judge,'
that we should bless 'Who is good and does good'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ כִּי חָסַר מִי מְבָרְכִינַן ״דַּיַּין הָאֱמֶת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא's suggestion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Comparison to the matching opposite ברכה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The moon growing is a benefit that deserves הטוב והמטיב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The good and bad ברכות go together, and we don't say the bad one for the moon, so we don't say the good one either.

steps.title: Then let us say both ברכות
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא replies: then say both, דיין האמת when it shrinks and הטוב והמטיב when it grows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let us say both of them!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא doesn't accept the answer. He suggests that maybe we should say both ברכות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא's answer showed only that the two ברכות go together. רב אחא turns this around: if they go together, then say both, and that would still mean saying הטוב והמטיב.

phrases.english: So let us bless both of them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's answer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Showing that the two ברכות go together doesn't remove either one. It could mean both should be said.

steps.title: It is the moon's normal way, so no ברכה
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that since growing and shrinking is the moon's regular nature, neither ברכה is said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since this is its normal way, we don't bless.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives his real reason. The moon's changes are completely normal, so they are not good or bad news that calls for these ברכות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הטוב והמטיב and דיין האמת are for something that actually happens to a person, good or bad. The moon growing and shrinking every month is just how nature works, so neither ברכה applies.
steps.whatToRemember: The moon gets ברכת הלבנה, not הטוב והמטיב or דיין האמת, because its changes are its normal nature and not news.

phrases.english: Since this is its normal way,
we do not bless.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of saying both ברכות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines what kind of event needs these ברכות
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Saying both ברכות would solve the problem.
steps.terutzMaskana: Regular, natural events don't get these ברכות at all.

steps.title: Blessing the month on time is like greeting the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that whoever says ברכת הלבנה at its proper time is like someone greeting the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא בר חנינא said in the name of רבי אסי, who said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Anyone who blesses the new month at its proper time is like someone who greets the Divine Presence.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins about how great ברכת הלבנה is. Saying it on time is like going out to greet the שכינה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a spiritual side to the ברכה. It is more than thanks for the moon; it is like standing before ה׳. The 'proper time' connects back to the time limits just discussed.

keyTerms.meaning: one who blesses the new month, meaning ברכת הלבנה

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main source for the special importance of ברכת הלבנה.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anyone who blesses the new month at its proper time
is as if he greets the face of the Divine Presence.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא בַּר חֲנִינָא אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching about the value of ברכת הלבנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying ברכת הלבנה at its proper time is like greeting the שכינה.

steps.title: The word 'this' links the month to seeing ה׳
steps.stepSummary: The source is the word 'זה' that appears in both the פסוק about the new month and the פסוק at the splitting of the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says here 'This month,' and it says there 'This is my God and I will glorify Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for רבי יוחנן's teaching. A shared word links two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the sea, the Jews could point at ה׳ and say 'This is my God.' The same word 'this' is used for the new month, which shows that seeing the new moon is also a kind of meeting ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is my God and I will glorify Him'

phrases.english: It is written here: 'This month,'
phrases.notes: שמות 12:2

phrases.english: and it is written there: 'This is my God and I will glorify Him.'
phrases.notes: שמות 15:2

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּתִיב הָכָא ״הַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה״ וּכְתִיב הָתָם ״זֶה אֵלִי וְאַנְוֵהוּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the פסוק source for step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That blessing the month is like greeting the שכינה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The shared word 'זה' in שמות 12:2 and שמות 15:2

steps.title: Once a month would have been enough
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא from the school of רבי ישמעאל says that greeting ה׳ once a month, through ברכת הלבנה, would have been enough of a privilege for the Jewish people.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: Even if the Jewish people had only the privilege of greeting their Father in Heaven once every month, it would be enough for them.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא backs up the idea that ברכת הלבנה is like greeting ה׳, and shows how big a privilege that is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This supports רבי יוחנן's idea from an older source. It describes the monthly ברכה as meeting 'their Father in Heaven,' a privilege great enough on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: the school of רבי ישמעאל taught

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
Even if the Jewish people had merited nothing
except to greet the face of their Father in Heaven
each and every month, it would be enough for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא that supports the idea in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: ברכת הלבנה is like greeting ה׳
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of the school of רבי ישמעאל

steps.title: So we say it standing
steps.stepSummary: אביי concludes that since the ברכה is like greeting the שכינה, it should be said standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Therefore, let us say it standing.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי draws a practical rule from the teachings above. You stand when greeting the שכינה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea of 'greeting the שכינה' becomes real הלכה. Just as one stands before an important person, one stands while saying ברכת הלבנה.
steps.whatToRemember: ברכת הלבנה is like greeting the שכינה, so it is said standing (אביי).

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Therefore, let us say it standing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical rule from steps 6 to 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ברכת הלבנה is said standing, out of respect for the שכינה.

steps.title: מרימר and מר זוטרא lean on each other while blessing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells that מרימר and מר זוטרא would lean on each other's shoulders while saying the ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: מרימר and מר זוטרא would lean on each other's shoulders and say the ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about how two אמוראים practiced ברכת הלבנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Coming right after אביי's rule, the story shows these אמוראים saying the ברכה while standing, leaning on each other for support.

phrases.english: Mareimar and Mar Zutra
would lean on each other's shoulders and bless.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָרִימָר וּמָר זוּטְרָא מְכַתְּפִי אַהֲדָדֵי וּמְבָרְכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows אביי's rule of standing in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Great אמוראים made the effort to stand for ברכת הלבנה, even supporting each other.

steps.title: The short ברכה used in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא tells רב אשי that in ארץ ישראל they say only 'ברוך מחדש חדשים'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא said to רב אשי: In the West they bless 'Blessed is He Who renews the months.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא brings up a shorter version of the ברכה used in ארץ ישראל. He seems to suggest it might be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The full ברכה is long. רב אחא reports a very short form, which raises the question of whether that short form is good enough for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: in the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha said to Rav Ashi:
In the West they bless: 'Blessed is He Who renews the months.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to the wording of the ברכה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the short ארץ ישראל form is a good enough ברכה.

steps.title: Even our women say that short version
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the short form is what even ordinary people, like our women, say. It is not the full ברכה expected of scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Our women also say that ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי waves off the short version. It is the simple form that people without much learning say, not the full ברכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying 'even our women say this,' רב אשי shows the short form is a basic version for everyday people. Someone who can say the full ברכה should not settle for it.
steps.whatToRemember: The short 'ברוך מחדש חדשים' is a basic form. The full ברכת הלבנה is expected of those who can say it.

phrases.english: He said to him:
That one, our women also bless.
phrases.notes: In other words, the short form is what anyone says; it isn't the full ברכה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רב אחא's report about the short ברכה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the short form is enough for learned people.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The short form is only the basic version said by those who don't know the full text.

steps.title: The full blessing follows רב יהודה's version
steps.stepSummary: Scholars should say the full ברכת הלבנה as רב יהודה wrote it, ending with 'מחדש חדשים'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, scholars say it like רב יהודה, who gave the full text: Blessed are You, Who by His word created the heavens and by the breath of His mouth all their hosts. He gave them a law and a set time so they would not change their task. They happily do their Owner's will. They are workers of truth whose work is truth. He told the moon to renew itself as a crown of beauty for the Jewish people, who will one day be renewed like it and praise their Creator. Blessed are You, ה׳, Who renews the months.
steps.whatsHappening: After רב אשי said the short form is only for ordinary people, the גמרא now gives the full ברכה that scholars should say: רב יהודה's version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The short line 'ברוך מחדש חדשים' is still included, but only as the closing line of a longer ברכה. The longer text praises the order of the heavens and compares the moon's renewal to the future renewal of the Jewish people.

keyTerms.meaning: Those carried from the womb, meaning the Jewish people
Who renews the months, the closing line of the ברכה

steps.whatToRemember: The full ברכת הלבנה is רב יהודה's version, and its closing line is 'ברוך אתה ה׳ מחדש חדשים'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source of the ברכת הלבנה text that is said today.

phrases.english: Rather, it is like the version of Rav Yehuda,
as Rav Yehuda said:
"Blessed [etc.], Who by His word created the heavens,
phrases.notes: The "etc." stands for the usual opening words: "are You, ה׳ our God, King of the world."

phrases.english: and by the breath of His mouth all their hosts.
He gave them a law and a set time
so that they would not change their task.
They are joyful and glad to do the will of their Owner.
They are workers of truth whose work is truth.
And to the moon He said that it should renew itself
as a crown of beauty for those carried from the womb,
phrases.notes: This means the Jewish people, whom ה׳ has carried since birth (ישעיהו 46:3).

phrases.english: who will one day be renewed like it
and will praise their Creator
for the honor of His kingship.
Blessed are You, ה׳, Who renews the months."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב אשי's reply by giving the full ברכה in place of the short form.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The full ברכה is רב יהודה's longer text, which closes with 'מחדש חדשים'.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Scholars say רב יהודה's full ברכת הלבנה.

steps.title: The war of Torah needs bundles of משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reads the פסוק about winning wars with strategy as meaning that only someone with a lot of משנה knowledge can succeed in Torah debate.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says, 'For with strategies you shall make your war.' רבי אחא בר חנינא said in the name of רבי אסי, quoting רבי יוחנן: Who can really fight the 'war' of Torah? Someone who holds 'bundles' of משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new, separate teaching that uses a פסוק to praise having a wide knowledge of משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תחבולות (strategies) is read as if it were חבילות (bundles). The idea is that a person needs a large store of basic sources before he can argue well in learning.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'war' of Torah, meaning the back-and-forth debate of learning
Bundles, here meaning a large amount of learned material

phrases.english: "For with strategies you shall make your war."
phrases.notes: משלי 24:6

phrases.english: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: בְּמִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא מִלְחַמְתָּהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה?
phrases.english: In whom do you find the war of Torah?
In one who has in his hand
bundles of Mishnah.
phrases.notes: Notice the wordplay: תחבולות (strategies) sounds like חבילות (bundles).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא בַּר חֲנִינָא אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic with no logical tie to ברכת הלבנה. It is brought here because it comes through the same chain as step 6: רבי אחא בר חנינא, quoting רבי אסי, quoting רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Success in Torah debate depends on first having a broad knowledge of משנה.

steps.title: רב יוסף applies a verse about the ox to himself
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף, who knew a great deal of משנה, read the פסוק about the strength of an ox as describing himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף used to apply this פסוק to himself: 'And much produce comes through the strength of the ox.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a short story that fits רבי יוחנן's teaching: רב יוסף saw his large store of knowledge as a source of great 'produce'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like a strong ox that brings in a big harvest, a person with a lot of learned material can produce a great deal of Torah. This supports the idea in the previous step.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef would read about himself:
"And much produce comes through the strength of the ox."
phrases.notes: משלי 14:4

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the previous teaching through a real person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Broad Torah knowledge is like an ox's strength, which brings a big harvest.

steps.title: Before sunrise versus after sunrise voids testimony
steps.stepSummary: Back to the משנה: a one-hour difference between witnesses is allowed, but רב שימי בר אשי says a disagreement over before or after sunrise voids the testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if one witness says 'at the second hour' and the other says 'at the third', the testimony stands. רב שימי בר אשי said: this is only about hours. But if one says it happened before sunrise and the other says after sunrise, their testimony is void.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about witnesses who disagree on the time, and רב שימי בר אשי sets a limit on the leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People easily mix up which hour it was, so a small gap in hours is forgiven. Before sunrise and after sunrise, though, are clearly different, so that kind of disagreement is a real contradiction and the testimony is voided.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this about (a limiting phrase)

phrases.english: "One says at two hours, etc."
phrases.notes: Back to the משנה: one witness says the second hour, the other the third, and the testimony still stands.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said:
They taught this only about hours,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אֶחָד אוֹמֵר קוֹדֶם הָנֵץ הַחַמָּה
phrases.english: but if one says before sunrise
and one says after sunrise,
their testimony is void.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שָׁעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה after the aggadic break.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A disagreement in hours is allowed, but disagreeing about before or after sunrise voids the testimony.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that רב שימי בר אשי's ruling is too obvious to need saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב שימי בר אשי: everyone knows dark and daylight are different, so why say it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אמורא's statement is expected to teach something new. Since nobody mixes up darkness with full sunlight, this ruling seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious! (a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new)

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the step before as teaching nothing new.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב שימי בר אשי's ruling about before versus after sunrise
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Before and after sunrise are clearly different, so obviously that is a real contradiction.

steps.title: The case is before sunrise versus during sunrise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording of רב שימי בר אשי's case: one witness says before sunrise and the other says during sunrise.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he meant: one says 'before sunrise' and the other says 'during sunrise'.
steps.whatsHappening: To answer the challenge, the גמרא changes the case to a closer pair of times: before sunrise and during sunrise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two times are now very close together, so it seems more possible that a witness made a mistake. Even so, רב שימי בר אשי voids the testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: During sunrise, while the sun is coming up

phrases.english: Rather: one says "before sunrise,"
and one says "during sunrise."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by changing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the statement to a less obvious case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב שימי בר אשי was talking about before sunrise versus after sunrise.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was talking about before sunrise versus during sunrise.

steps.title: Isn't this also obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the new case is still obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: This too is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes again: before sunrise and during sunrise are still different moments, so why does this need saying?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even with the changed case, the witnesses are describing two different stages of the day. So the גמרא asks again what new idea רב שימי בר אשי is teaching.

phrases.english: This too is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the changed case with the same 'obvious' challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The changed case of before versus during sunrise
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These are still two different moments, so the contradiction seems plain.

steps.title: We might have thought he only saw an early glow
steps.stepSummary: The ruling was needed because we might have excused the witness who said 'during sunrise' as having seen only a glow from an open spot. רב שימי בר אשי teaches that we do not assume this.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: the witness who said 'during sunrise' was standing in an open place and only saw an early glow, so the two witnesses do not really disagree. So he teaches us that the testimony is still void.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what is new in the ruling: we do not invent an excuse to make the two witnesses agree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One could think the 'during sunrise' witness saw the first rays from an open spot, so both witnesses describe the same moment. רב שימי בר אשי rejects that idea and treats the testimony as contradictory, so it is void.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken idea)
Rays or a glow of light
He teaches us (that the mistaken idea is wrong)

steps.whatToRemember: If witnesses disagree about before sunrise versus during sunrise, the testimony is void. We do not assume one of them just saw an early glow.

phrases.english: You might have said:
this one was standing in an open place,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the witness who said "during sunrise."

phrases.english: and it was just a glow of light that he saw,
so he teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second 'obvious' challenge by showing the mistake the ruling prevents.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: showing a reasonable mistake the ruling prevents
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We would excuse the witness by saying he saw an early glow from an open spot, so the witnesses agree.
steps.terutzMaskana: We do not assume that. The testimony counts as contradictory and is void.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Before sunrise versus during sunrise is a real contradiction that voids the testimony.

steps.title: Only that day? A ברייתא says he can stay forever
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about the student who argues for acquittal and stays seated with the judges all that day. It challenges this with a ברייתא: if his point has substance, he never comes down at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says the student who offers a reason to acquit sits with the judges and doesn't come down that day. Only that day and no longer? But a ברייתא teaches: if his words have substance, he never comes down. If they have no substance, he still stays the whole day, so that his going up should not turn into an embarrassing going down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and points out that it seems to clash with a ברייתא about how long the student stays seated among the judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה limits the student's seat to 'that day'. The ברייתא splits into two cases: a good point earns him a permanent seat, and a weak point still earns him one full day so he is not shamed. So the משנה's 'that day' looks too short.

keyTerms.meaning: going up (here, being raised to sit with the judges)

phrases.english: And afterward they bring in, etc.
phrases.notes: The גמרא is pointing to the משנה here. The part it really means comes later: the student who argues for acquittal is seated with the judges all day.

phrases.english: That day and no more?
But isn't it taught:
If there is substance in his words,
he would never come down from there,
and if there is no substance in his words,
he does not come down the whole day,

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא תְּהֵא עֲלִיָּיתוֹ יְרִידָה לוֹ.
phrases.english: so that his going up should not be a going down for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of the witnesses' timing and goes back to a later line in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that the student stays seated only 'that day'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says a student with a good point stays forever, so 'that day' cannot be the rule for every student.

steps.title: אביי: The משנה means a student whose point had no substance
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the משנה is talking about the case where the student's argument had no real substance.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Read the משנה as talking about the case where his words have no substance.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by narrowing which case the משנה is describing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the משנה is read as describing a student with a weak point, it matches the second half of the ברייתא: he stays one full day to spare him shame. The case of a good point, where he stays forever, is simply not what the משנה is discussing.
steps.whatToRemember: A student who argues for acquittal stays forever if his point is good. If it is weak, he stays one day so he is not embarrassed. The משנה is describing the weak case.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Explain it
as referring to when there is no substance in his words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (the משנה refers to only one of the ברייתא's cases)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's 'that day' seemed to cover every student.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה refers only to a student whose point lacked substance.

steps.title: Why may the judges not drink wine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה again and asks why the judges may not drink wine on the day of the trial.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: if they found a reason to acquit him, etc. Wine: what is the reason they don't drink it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind the משנה's rule that the judges avoid wine. The next step gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the judges do not drink wine all day while a capital case is still open. The גמרא wants the basis for this rule.

phrases.english: They found a reason to acquit him, etc.
phrases.notes: The line being asked about comes next in the משנה: the judges don't drink wine all day.

phrases.english: Wine: what is the reason they do not drink it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new detail in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the rule that judges in a capital case may not drink wine.

steps.title: רבי אחא בר חנינא: 'Princes' deal with deep matters and must not get drunk
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא בר חנינא brings a פסוק about princes (רוזנים) and reads it as 'those who deal with the secret (רז) of the world'. They must not become drunk.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא בר חנינא said: The פסוק says 'nor for princes (רוזנים) to say: where is strong drink'. This means that those who deal with the secret of the world should not get drunk.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אחא בר חנינא answers the question by finding the rule in a פסוק through a play on words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word רוזנים, 'princes', sounds like רז, 'secret'. So the פסוק is read as speaking to people who handle the world's weightiest matters, like judges deciding life and death. They must stay sober.

keyTerms.meaning: the secret of the world (weighty, serious matters)

phrases.english: Rabbi Aḥa bar Ḥanina said:
The verse says:
"Nor for princes: where is strong drink"
phrases.notes: משלי 31:4. Listen for רוזנים sounding like רז, 'secret'.

phrases.english: those who deal with the secret of the world
should not become drunk.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא בַּר חֲנִינָא: אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about wine.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is משלי 31:4, read as 'those dealing with the world's secret must not get drunk'.

steps.title: What if the judges never come to agree?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה again and asks what happens if none of the judges who vote to convict ever comes around to the side that acquits.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: if they found a reason to acquit him, etc. If they do not see it, what happens?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about a deadlocked court, a case the משנה does not spell out. The next step answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that when the court is stuck, the judges keep discussing until one of those who wants to convict sees the point of those who acquit. The גמרא asks what happens if that never happens.

keyTerms.meaning: they did not see (they were not convinced)

phrases.english: They found a reason to acquit him, etc.
If they did not see it, what happens?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question on a different part of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the court does if the judges stay deadlocked.

steps.title: רבי אחא and רבי יוחנן: They set him free
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא rules that a deadlocked court sets the defendant free, and רבי יוחנן says the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא said: They set him free. And רבי יוחנן also said: They set him free.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question in the same way: if the judges never agree, the defendant goes free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No majority to convict was ever reached, so the defendant was never found guilty and is released. רבי יוחנן's matching statement backs up רבי אחא.

phrases.english: Rabbi Aḥa said: They release him.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: פּוֹטְרִין אוֹתוֹ.
phrases.english: And likewise Rabbi Yoḥanan said: They release him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the deadlock question.

steps.title: רב פפא: Then why not free him right away?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks אביי: if a deadlock ends with the defendant going free anyway, why not free him at the start instead of arguing on?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: Then let them set him free from the beginning!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא challenges the point of the long discussion if it ends in release anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a deadlock ends in release, all the arguing seems pointless. The court could just free him as soon as it sees it is stuck.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
Then let them release him from the start!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning behind the ruling just given.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's requirement to keep discussing, now that we know a deadlock ends in release.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the result is release either way, the extra discussion seems useless.

steps.title: אביי: So the court does not walk out confused
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes רבי יוחנן: the judges keep discussing so that they don't leave the court in confusion, without a clear result.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: so that they should not leave the בית דין confused.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains why the discussion matters even though a deadlock ends in release.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion is not mainly about changing the result. It is about the court ending with a clear decision instead of walking out muddled, which would make the בית דין look bad.
steps.whatToRemember: A deadlocked court sets the defendant free. Still, the judges keep discussing first, so the בית דין does not end in confusion.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יֵצְאוּ מִבֵּית דִּין מְעוּרְבָּבִין.
phrases.english: so that they should not leave the court confused.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יֵצְאוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the purpose of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The discussion seemed pointless if release follows anyway.
steps.terutzMaskana: The discussion lets the court end with clarity instead of confusion.

steps.title: Second version: why add judges at all?
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, רב פפא asks אביי why the court adds judges at all instead of freeing the defendant from the first court.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the conversation went like this: רב פפא said to אביי, why do we need to add judges? Let the first court just set him free!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the רב פפא and אביי conversation. In this version רב פפא challenges the whole idea of adding judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version (step 27), רב פפא asked why the judges keep arguing when a deadlock frees the defendant anyway. Here his question goes further back. If the first court could not convict him, why add more judges at all? Just free him right away.

keyTerms.meaning: They shall add (more judges to the court)
Let them release him, set him free
The first court, before any judges were added

phrases.english: Some say:
Rav Pappa said to Abaye,
But why do I need them to add judges?
Let them release him from the first court!

steps.triggerLanguage: איכא דאמרי: אמר ליה רב פפא לאביי, ולמה לי יוסיפו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of the challenge in step 27, now aimed at the משנה's rule of adding judges.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that judges are added when the court is undecided
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a court that cannot convict ends up freeing the defendant anyway, adding judges seems pointless. Free him from the first court.

steps.title: אביי: רבי יוסי agrees with you
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that רבי יוסי holds like רב פפא: judges are not added, not to a court of 71 and not to a court of 23.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: רבי יוסי agrees with you. As a ברייתא teaches: רבי יוסי says, just as we do not add judges to a court of seventy-one, so too we do not add judges to a court of twenty-three.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי does not argue with רב פפא. He shows that a תנא, רבי יוסי, already holds exactly what רב פפא suggested.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that the סנהדרין of 71 never gets extra judges. רבי יוסי compares the court of 23 to it: no judges are added there either. So if the court of 23 cannot convict, the defendant goes free. רב פפא's idea is a real opinion, though the משנה follows a different view.

keyTerms.meaning: Stands with you, holds like your opinion
The court of seventy-one (the great סנהדרין)
The court of twenty-three, which judges capital cases

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוסי, no judges are ever added, not to the court of 71 and not to the court of 23. If the court of 23 cannot reach a verdict, the defendant goes free.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Rabbi Yosei stands with you,
as it is taught in a ברייתא:
Rabbi Yosei says,
just as they do not add judges

phrases.aramaic: עַל בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל שִׁבְעִים וְאֶחָד,
phrases.english: to a court of seventy-one,
so too they do not add judges

phrases.aramaic: עַל בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה.
phrases.english: to a court of twenty-three.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה: רבי יוסי קאי כוותך, דתניא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 29 by agreeing with it and pointing to a תנא who holds that way.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Concession: the challenge matches a real opinion (רבי יוסי) that differs from the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Adding judges seemed to be a fixed rule that everyone holds
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוסי holds that no judges are added even to a court of 23, just as with the court of 71

steps.title: The phrase "the judgment has grown old"
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that in money cases the judges say נזדקן הדין, but in capital cases they do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: in money cases one says "the judgment has grown old," but in capital cases one does not say "the judgment has grown old."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a phrase the judges announce, which is said in money cases but not in capital cases. This sets up the next question about what the phrase means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives the rule but does not explain the phrase. Since we don't know what "grown old" means, we can't yet tell why it fits money cases and not capital cases. The next steps try to work that out.

keyTerms.meaning: The judgment has grown old, a phrase the judges announce
Capital cases, where a life is at stake

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
In money cases one says
"The judgment has grown old,"
but in capital cases one does not say
"The judgment has grown old."

steps.triggerLanguage: תנו רבנן: אומר בדיני ממונות נזדקן הדין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, still about how a court handles reaching a verdict.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The phrase נזדקן הדין is said in money cases but not in capital cases.

steps.title: If it means "the case is stuck," the rule seems backwards
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what נזדקן הדין means. If it means the case has dragged on and needs more time, then the ברייתא should say it about capital cases, not money cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does "the judgment has grown old" mean? If you say it means "the case has gotten old," meaning it is stuck, then he should have said the reverse!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the phrase means. It tries one meaning and shows that this meaning makes the ברייתא look backwards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If "grown old" means the case is stuck and needs more discussion, that need matters most when a life is at stake. So the phrase should be said in capital cases. The ברייתא says the opposite, and that is the problem.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say: introduces a suggested explanation
The case has gotten old, meaning it is stuck and needs more time
He should have said the reverse

phrases.english: What does "the judgment has grown old" mean?
If you say: the case has gotten old,
phrases.notes: קש means old. Here that means the case is dragging on and needs more discussion.

phrases.english: he should have said the reverse!

steps.triggerLanguage: מאי נזדקן הדין? אילימא קש דינא, איפכא מיבעיא ליה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the phrase in step 31 means and challenges one possible reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading נזדקן הדין as "the case is stuck"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: More discussion is needed most in capital cases, so the phrase should be said there, the opposite of what the ברייתא says.

steps.title: First answer: reverse the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר מנוח, quoting רב אחא son of רב איקא, says to switch the ברייתא: the phrase is said in capital cases, not in money cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר מנוח said in the name of רב אחא son of רב איקא: reverse it.
steps.whatsHappening: This answer keeps the meaning "the case is stuck" and fixes the ברייתא by switching its two halves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the ברייתא reads: in capital cases one says "the case is stuck" and more time is given, but in money cases one does not. This matches the idea that a life deserves extra care.

keyTerms.meaning: Reverse it, switch the two parts of the statement

phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Manoach said

phrases.aramaic: מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא:
phrases.english: in the name of Rav Acha son of Rav Ika:
Reverse it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב הונא בר מנוח משמיה דרב אחא בריה דרב איקא: איפוך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 32 by switching the halves of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the text: swap the two halves of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא as written says the phrase only in money cases
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase "the case is stuck" is said in capital cases, where more time is given, and not in money cases

steps.title: רב אשי: keep the ברייתא, it means "the case has grown wise"
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי keeps the ברייתא as written and explains that נזדקן הדין means the case has grown wise, meaning it has been fully discussed and is ready for a vote.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: really, do not reverse it. What does "the judgment has grown old" mean? The case has grown wise.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different answer. He changes the meaning of the phrase instead of changing the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An old person, a זקן, is wise. So "the case has grown old" means the case has been fully discussed and it is time to decide. Ending the discussion is fine in money cases. In capital cases, the judges keep looking for a way to save the defendant, so they don't announce it. The ברייתא now makes sense without any change.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, do not reverse it: keep the text as it is
The case has grown wise: it is fully discussed and ready for a verdict

steps.confusionAlert: The same phrase, נזדקן הדין, means opposite things in the two answers. For רב הונא בר מנוח it means "the case is stuck, we need more time." For רב אשי it means "the case is ready, let's decide."

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Really, do not reverse it,
and what does "the judgment has grown old" mean?
The case has grown wise.
phrases.notes: Think of an elder who has gained wisdom. The case has been talked through and is ready for a vote.

steps.triggerLanguage: רב אשי אמר: לעולם לא תיפוך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 32 that disagrees with step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New meaning for the term, with no change to the text
steps.terutzHavaAmina: נזדקן הדין means the case is stuck, so the ברייתא looks backwards
steps.terutzMaskana: נזדקן הדין means the case has grown wise and is ready for a verdict, which fits money cases and not capital cases

steps.title: Challenge: the greatest judge would not announce something embarrassing
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the greatest judge announces נזדקן הדין. That fits "the case has grown wise," but it does not fit "the case is stuck," since he would not embarrass himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: the greatest of the judges says "the judgment has grown old." If you say it means "the case has grown wise," that is why the greatest says it. But if you say it means "the case is stuck," is there no way except for the greatest to say it? Should he embarrass himself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to attack the reading "the case is stuck" used by רב הונא בר מנוח in step 33.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Announcing that a case is ready for a decision is an honor, so the head judge would be the one to say it. Announcing that the court is stuck is embarrassing, and the head judge would not be the one to say it about himself. So the ברייתא fits רב אשי's reading and raises a problem for the other one.

keyTerms.meaning: The greatest of the judges, the head of the court
It works well if you say: introduces the reading that fits

steps.whatToRemember: In this first version, the ברייתא about the greatest judge fits רב אשי's reading ("the case has grown wise") and challenges the reading "the case is stuck." The next step answers the challenge.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
The greatest of the judges says "the judgment has grown old."
It works well if you say it means "the case has grown wise,"
that is why the greatest one says it.
But if you say it means "the case is stuck,"
is there no way except for the greatest one to say it?
Should he embarrass himself?

steps.triggerLanguage: מיתיבי: גדול שבדיינין אומר נזדקן הדין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading in step 33 ("the case is stuck") and fits רב אשי's reading in step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of נזדקן הדין as "the case is stuck" (step 33)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says the head judge announces the phrase. He would gladly announce an honorable result ("the case is wise"), but he would not announce that his own court is stuck.

steps.title: Yes, the greatest judge says it, because self-embarrassment is easier
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends the 'case is stuck' reading. Even if נזדקן הדין admits that the court is stuck, the greatest judge should say it, because it is better to embarrass yourself than to be embarrassed by others.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, he says it anyway. Being embarrassed by yourself is not the same as being embarrassed by others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 35. It says that yes, the greatest judge announces that the case is stuck, even though it is embarrassing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 35 argued that the greatest judge would never announce 'we are stuck,' because it would shame him. The answer accepts that it is shameful but says it is less painful if he says it himself. If a junior judge said it, the greatest judge would be shamed by others, which is worse.

phrases.english: Yes.
One who is embarrassed by himself is not comparable
to one who is embarrassed by others.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין. אֵינוֹ דּוֹמֶה מִתְבַּיֵּישׁ מֵעַצְמוֹ לְמִתְבַּיֵּישׁ מֵאֲחֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 35 against the 'case is stuck' reading.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the premise (it is embarrassing) but shows it still makes sense for the greatest judge to say it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The greatest judge would avoid saying something that shames him.
steps.terutzMaskana: Shame that comes from yourself is lighter than shame that comes from others, so he prefers to say it himself.

steps.title: Second version: the challenge is turned against the 'grown wise' reading
steps.stepSummary: Another version of the discussion reverses the challenge. The 'stuck' reading fits fine, but if נזדקן הדין means 'the case has grown wise,' the greatest judge would be praising himself, and the פסוק says not to praise yourself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say it went like this: It makes sense if you say it means 'the case has aged,' since being embarrassed by yourself is not like being embarrassed by others. But if you say it means 'the case has grown wise,' should the greatest judge praise himself? It is written: 'Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version (איכא דאמרי) of the challenge from the ברייתא. This time the challenge targets רב אשי's reading, 'the case has grown wise.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version the 'stuck' reading has no problem, for the reason given in step 36. The difficulty is with רב אשי: announcing 'the case has grown wise' sounds like the greatest judge is praising the court's wisdom, including his own. That seems to go against the פסוק in משלי that forbids praising yourself.

keyTerms.meaning: The case has aged, meaning it is stuck
The case has grown wise, meaning it is fully discussed
Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth

steps.confusionAlert: In the first version the challenge hit the 'stuck' reading. In this איכא דאמרי it hits the 'grown wise' reading. Same ברייתא, opposite target.

phrases.english: Some say:
It works well if you say 'the case has aged,'
phrases.notes: 'Aged' here is the 'stuck, needs more time' reading from step 33.

phrases.english: that is why: one embarrassed by himself is not comparable
to one embarrassed by others.
But if you say 'the case has grown wise,'
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי's reading from step 34.

phrases.english: should the greatest judge praise himself?
But it is written: 'Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth'!
phrases.notes: משלי 27:2

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא קַשׁ דִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of step 35's challenge, now aimed at רב אשי instead of the 'stuck' reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's reading that נזדקן הדין means 'the case has grown wise.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the phrase praises the court's wisdom, the greatest judge saying it would be self-praise, which the פסוק in משלי rules out. The ברייתא says he does say it, so the reading seems wrong.

steps.title: Court business is the greatest judge's job
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that court matters are different. Running the court is the greatest judge's responsibility, so his announcement is not self-praise.
steps.simpleTranslation: A court matter is different, because it is the responsibility of the greatest judge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב אשי's reading. It explains that the greatest judge says it because that is his official job, not to praise himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק forbids praising yourself in ordinary life. In court, announcements are part of the greatest judge's role, so his words are court procedure, not boasting. This saves the reading 'the case has grown wise.'

keyTerms.meaning: Is placed upon, is the responsibility of

phrases.english: A matter of the court is different,
since it rests upon the greatest judge.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי מִילְּתָא דְּבֵי דִינָא דְּאַגָּדוֹל רַמְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 37 against רב אשי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: court announcements are an official duty, not personal self-praise.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The greatest judge announcing 'the case has grown wise' would be self-praise.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since court matters are his responsibility, the announcement is part of his role and is allowed.

steps.title: Proof from the משנה: the greatest judge announces the verdict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its answer with a משנה: after the judges finish, they bring in the litigants, and the greatest judge announces who is exempt and who is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: When they finished the matter, they would bring them in. The greatest of the judges says: 'So-and-so, you are exempt,' 'So-and-so, you are liable.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to prove that court announcements are the greatest judge's job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה shows that the greatest judge, not just any judge, announces the final verdict to the litigants. That proves that speaking for the court is his role. So when he says נזדקן הדין, he is doing his job, not praising himself.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה

steps.whatToRemember: Both readings of נזדקן הדין survive. 'Stuck' works because shame from yourself is easier. 'Grown wise' works because speaking for the court is the greatest judge's job, as the משנה about announcing verdicts shows.

phrases.english: As we learned in a משנה:
When they finished the matter,
they would bring them in.
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the two sides in the case, who wait outside while the judges discuss.

phrases.english: The greatest of the judges says:
'So-and-so, you are exempt,'
'So-and-so, you are liable.'

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדִתְנַן: גָּמְרוּ אֶת הַדָּבָר הָיוּ מַכְנִיסִין אוֹתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to back up the answer of step 38.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that court announcements are the greatest judge's responsibility.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה (סנהדרין 29a) in which the greatest judge announces the verdict to the litigants.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter היו בודקין
steps.stepSummary: The פרק הָיוּ בּוֹדְקִין ends with the traditional הדרן formula.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'They would examine.'
steps.whatsHappening: This line is the formal closing of the chapter. It is not part of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן is a traditional farewell said at the end of each chapter, showing our wish to come back and learn it again. The chapter is named after its opening words, הָיוּ בּוֹדְקִין, about examining the witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They would examine,' the name of the chapter

phrases.english: We will return to you, 'They would examine'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter after the final discussion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק הָיוּ בּוֹדְקִין is complete.
